name: Azithromycin
summary: Broad macrolide for respiratory and skin infections with atypical pathogen coverage; long half-life allows short courses.
mechanism: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (blocks translocation).
pharmacodynamics: Time-dependent killing with a prolonged post-antibiotic effect; extensive tissue distribution with levels exceeding serum.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic — minimal CYP metabolism (mostly excreted unchanged)

dosing.adult: 500 mg PO on day 1, then 250 mg PO once daily on days 2-5 (respiratory/skin infections); 2 g PO single dose for chlamydia

safety.pregnancy: Generally considered safe (category B); widely used
safety.lactation: Compatible — excreted in breast milk but considered low risk
contraindications: Prior cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction with azithromycin
warnings: QT prolongation (esp. with other QT-prolonging drugs or hypokalemia)
monitoring: LFTs in patients with hepatic disease

clinicalPearls: Long half-life allows a 5-day (or single-dose) course
Active against atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia pneumoniae)
good: Short-course, once-daily oral therapy with atypical pathogen coverage.
bad: QT prolongation risk, growing macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae, and limited Gram-negative activity.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard infectious-disease/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
